props.title: Seven Brides for Seven Brothers
props.initialSlug: Dancing frontiersmen plot to kidnap their brides

sections.content: Seven Brides for Seven Brothers (1954) revolutionized the movie musical with Michael Kidd's athletic, masculine choreography that merged ballet with backwoods brawling. The barn-raising dance sequence remains one of cinema's most impressive set pieces, with acrobatic moves performed by actual dancers on real logs and beams. Director Stanley Donen, fresh off co-directing Singin' in the Rain (1952), brought his innovative camera movements to the Oregon wilderness, creating dynamic musical numbers that influenced everything from West Side Story (1961) to La La Land (2016).

sections.content: The film's problematic plot, based loosely on the Roman legend of the Sabine women, gets reimagined through Howard Keel and Jane Powell's charismatic performances. Their chemistry in numbers like "Wonderful, Wonderful Day" and "When You're in Love" helps soften the dated gender politics. The success of Seven Brides sparked a wave of rustic Americana musicals like Paint Your Wagon (1969) and influenced the robust dancing style seen in The Music Man (1962). SUBHEAD: Innovation in Dance and Musical Storytelling

Michael Kidd's choreography broke new ground by incorporating realistic movements into dance numbers. Unlike the purely balletic approach of An American in Paris (1951) or the tap-heavy Top Hat (1935), Kidd had his dancers perform moves that mountain men might actually do - chopping wood, raising barns, and even fighting. This naturalistic approach influenced later choreographers like Jerome Robbins in West Side Story (1961) and Bob Fosse in Sweet Charity (1969).
